Vatsalya: Reading the Curve Before the Festival Spend

Case lens: retention curves and the product-market-fit signal. Does the curve flatten — and if it flattens for only some users, what should the company do with the rest?

1. The Friday deadline

On the morning of Friday, 10 July 2026, Divya Menon sat in Vatsalya's office off 12th Main in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with two charts open on one screen and a budget sheet on the other. The budget sheet said ₹18 crore. It was the money the board had released for the second half of the financial year, and the board had asked for an allocation plan by the following Friday, 17 July, so that any festive media buying could be booked before Onam and Ganesh Chaturthi rates hardened.

Divya had been Vatsalya's vice-president of product for twenty months. The charts on her screen were the reason she had not slept well. The first showed monthly active users rising from 310,000 to 690,000 over eleven months. The second showed what happened to the parents who had joined in a single week of January, followed forward to July. Only one of those two charts was going to be right about whether Vatsalya deserved ₹18 crore of growth spending.

2. Vatsalya

Vatsalya was founded in 2022 by a paediatrician and a former engineering manager who had met at a parenting group in Koramangala. The app served Indian parents of children from birth to five years. Its core was a daily card: a two-minute developmental activity matched to the child's age in weeks, written in English, Hindi, Marathi, Tamil and Malayalam, with a short audio version for parents who preferred listening while feeding. Around that core sat a milestone tracker, a moderated community, a paediatrician question queue answered within twenty-four hours, and a small commerce shelf selling weaning bowls, sensory toys and picture books.

The company had raised ₹96 crore across two rounds. It made money three ways: a ₹399-per-quarter ad-free and unlimited-question tier, commerce margin averaging 22 per cent on a basket of ₹1,240, and brand partnerships with baby-care marketers. Revenue for the year to March 2026 was ₹38 crore.

The competitive picture was crowded and unsentimental. FirstCry owned the commerce relationship with Indian parents at a scale Vatsalya could not approach; Amazon and Flipkart carried the same categories with faster delivery; Nykaa had built a strong position in mother-and-baby care; Meesho supplied the price-sensitive end. On the content and consultation side, Practo and Apollo 24|7 had trained Indian families to expect a doctor on a phone. Vatsalya's claim was narrower: that a parent with an eight-week-old baby at 2 a.m. wants a specific, trustworthy, two-minute thing to do, and that no marketplace was built for that moment.

Regulation shaped the product more than the founders had expected. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 required verifiable parental consent for processing children's data and prohibited tracking and behaviourally targeted advertising directed at children. Vatsalya had responded by keeping all child data under the parent's account, by refusing third-party ad SDKs entirely, and by building its own consent ledger — a ₹2.9 crore programme that had cost it two quarters of feature work and, Divya believed, was the main reason brand partners trusted it.

3. The situation

In April 2026, Rohit Bagchi, Vatsalya's data scientist, working from Toronto, rebuilt the retention reporting. The old dashboard had counted an app open as activity. Rohit's version counted a completed daily card — the parent had opened the card and marked it done or played the audio to the end — on the argument that a parenting app that is opened and closed has not helped anybody.

Under the new definition the blended curve fell from 100 per cent to 19 per cent over twelve weeks and then sat between 18 and 19 per cent for three months. Read on its own, that looked like a floor, and Vatsalya's chief executive, Arjun Rao, read it exactly that way. Rohit did not. He split the cohort by the age of the child at sign-up, and the single line became two entirely different products, shown in Exhibit 1.

The split had an obvious explanation, and it had been in front of the team for years without being named. A parent of a newborn faces a new, urgent and unfamiliar question almost every day: feeding, sleep, a rash, a missed milestone. A parent of a four-year-old faces one every few weeks. The natural frequency of the problem was simply different at the two ends of the age range, and a daily card was the right shape for only one of them.

The team saw this from four cities and did not agree about what it meant. Lena Fischer, the design lead in Berlin, had spent March redesigning the card for older children and read the flat blended line as evidence her work had landed. Adeline Tan, who ran community and support from Singapore, saw the opposite in her queue: almost every message that thanked the product came from a parent in the first year. Vikram Nair, who handled diaspora partnerships from New Jersey and had a Dubai retail tie-up with a large Indian-origin grocery chain waiting on signature, wanted volume above all, because his partner's minimum guarantee was written against installs.

6. The options

Option A — spend for scale. Put ₹12 crore into festive acquisition on the current mix, hold the blended 18.6 per cent floor as the retention story, reach roughly 1.4 million monthly actives by March and open the Series C conversation on volume. The upside is that Vikram's Dubai guarantee is met, brand sponsorship pricing holds, and the growth chart stays unbroken. The cost is that, on Exhibit 2's arithmetic, about ₹8 crore of the ₹12 crore buys parents who will be gone by week twenty-six, and any investor who asks for the cohort split during diligence will find Exhibit 1.

Option B — narrow to the segment that flattens. Re-point acquisition at parents of infants through antenatal classes, paediatric clinics and hospital tie-ups at ₹375 a registration, fund Adeline's paediatrician capacity, and make the company's single product goal the share of new parents who complete a card on four of their first seven days. The upside is that every rupee buys a parent who stays, contribution per registration rises from a blended ₹115 to something near ₹309, and the retention story survives diligence. The cost is that registrations fall by roughly half, the monthly active chart flattens, the Dubai guarantee is missed or renegotiated, and Arjun has to tell the board a smaller number.

Option C — build a second product for the second segment. Accept that a daily card is the wrong shape for a parent of a four-year-old and spend ₹3.8 crore building a weekly digest with a different natural frequency — school-readiness, behaviour, nutrition — while holding acquisition flat. The upside is that it addresses the real cause rather than the symptom and, if it works, doubles the addressable base. The cost is two quarters of engineering, a second curve to prove from scratch, and the risk that the team ends up with two products and fit in neither.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Vatsalya's blended retention has been between 18 and 19 per cent for three months. Why is that not evidence of product-market fit, and what exactly does Exhibit 1 show that the blended line conceals?

2. The infant segment flattens at 61 per cent and the older segment does not flatten at all. How much of that difference is attributable to the product, and how much to the natural frequency of the problem each parent has?

3. Using Exhibits 2 and 3, what is the contribution consequence of Option A versus Option B over the next twelve months? What would have to be true for Option A to be the better decision?

4. What should Divya recommend on 17 July, what will she say to Vikram about the Dubai guarantee, and what single number should Vatsalya report to its board as its retention figure from now on?

8. A note for the learner

This case turns on one idea: a flattening retention curve is the only real signal of product-market fit, and a blended curve that looks flat is not the same thing as a flat curve. Vatsalya's 18.6 per cent line stopped falling for an arithmetic reason rather than a behavioural one. As the older-child segment decayed towards zero, its weight in the average shrank, so the average drifted towards the infant segment's stable 61 per cent and appeared to settle. No parent's behaviour changed at week twelve. Whenever a blended floor appears at roughly the point where one segment is nearly extinct, that is the first thing to test.

The second idea is that the shape a curve can take is constrained by how often the underlying problem occurs. A parent of an eight-week-old has a question most days; a parent of a four-year-old does not. A daily card can only build a habit where a daily need exists. That is not a failure of Lena's design work; it is a mismatch between the product's rhythm and the problem's rhythm, and no amount of craft on the card will fix it.

A well-reasoned answer therefore does three things. It reports the segment curves rather than the blend. It treats the 61 per cent infant floor as a genuine product-market-fit claim — narrow, but real and defensible in diligence. And it separates the question "where should acquisition money go?" from the question "should we build something for the other segment?", because Exhibit 2 answers the first decisively and says nothing about the second.

One defensible path: Divya recommends Option B as the allocation and Option C as a bounded experiment. She commits ₹12 crore to infant-led acquisition and ₹2.6 crore to paediatrician capacity, which protects the segment that actually retains and relieves the support backlog that threatens it. She ring-fences ₹1.5 crore — not ₹3.8 crore — for a twelve-week test of the weekly digest with 20,000 existing older-child parents, with a stated pass mark agreed in advance: a week-twelve bounded retention above 25 per cent on the new weekly action. If it passes, the remaining ₹2.3 crore follows in the next quarter; if it fails, Vatsalya stops acquiring that segment altogether.

On the Dubai guarantee, she goes to Vikram with the contribution arithmetic before she goes to the partner, and proposes renegotiating the minimum from 250,000 registrations to a smaller number of registrations plus a revenue share, on the grounds that a guarantee written against installs is a guarantee written against the wrong number. The board hears a smaller growth figure and a retention claim that will survive being checked. That is the trade the case asks the reader to weigh, and reasonable people can defend Option A if they believe the Series C window closes before the narrow story can compound.

Retention Curves and the PMF Signal

A flattening curve is the strongest product-market-fit evidence a product team can produce. It is also, on close inspection, one of the most reliably misread charts in the discipline.

1. Two decisions, six weeks apart

On Tuesday, 21 April 2026, Devika Raghunathan, VP Product at Sulagti Labs in Pune, was asked by her chief executive to write one sentence for a Series A extension memo. Sulagti sold an AI drafting assistant to chartered-accountancy firms: paste in a GST notice, and the product produced a reply with the relevant sections, the firm's own prior filings, and the arithmetic reconciled. Two thousand three hundred firms had paid for at least one month at ₹2,400 per seat. The first large activated cohort, from March 2025, had fallen to 23.7% by month twelve and had since moved barely half a percentage point a month. The chief executive wanted the sentence to read: "Sulagti has product-market fit; the retention curve has flattened at 24%." Devika believed the number was accurate and the sentence was false, and she had four days to explain why in a way that did not sound like an analyst hedging.

On Friday, 7 August 2026, in Coimbatore, Prakash Sundaram, co-founder and chief product officer of Angaarpeth Energy, faced a different version of the same trap. Angaarpeth sold a ₹2,490 clip-on energy monitor that sat on a household or workshop meter and streamed consumption to a phone app; 61,000 units had shipped since January 2025 across Coimbatore, Tiruppur and Erode. His growth lead had proposed a ₹99-a-month "Plus" analytics tier and had built the revenue model on the device retention curve, which had flattened beautifully at 85% of devices still reporting nine months after installation. Prakash had a second curve on the same cohort — app engagement — that flattened at 7%. Both curves were correct. Only one of them described a business the subscription could be sold into, and the board meeting was in eleven days.

These two scenes frame the argument of this page. The retention curve is the best instrument product management has for the question "have we built something people keep choosing?" — and almost every serious error made with it comes from treating the shape of the line as the evidence, when the evidence is actually in the rate underneath the line, the definition behind the axis, and the population inside the cohort.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Formally, a retention curve is an empirical survival function. Take a cohort — the set of users who first performed the product's core value action in some window — and let S(t) be the proportion of that cohort who perform the core action again during period t measured from their own start. S(0) = 1 by construction, and S(t) falls. The associated quantity, and the one that does the real work, is the conditional or period-over-period retention rate r(t) = S(t)/S(t−1): of the people still with you last period, what fraction stayed this period. Its complement, 1 − r(t), is the discrete hazard. The survival curve is the visible artefact; the hazard is the mechanism.

The technique is borrowed, not invented. Life tables date to seventeenth-century mortality work and were industrialised by actuaries; medical statistics formalised them as Kaplan–Meier estimation in 1958, with the machinery for censored observations that product analytics quietly relies on and rarely names. Marketing science imported the logic into customer-base analysis from the 1980s onward. The specific product-management claim — that a flattening cohort curve is the operational definition of product-market fit — crystallised in Silicon Valley's growth literature in the early 2010s, out of work by practitioners including Sean Ellis, Brian Balfour and Andrew Chen, in reaction to a concrete pathology: companies raising capital on download counts and monthly actives that were being backfilled by paid acquisition faster than cohorts were decaying. The retention curve was invented, in product management, to make that particular lie impossible to tell with a straight face.

Four schools now share the vocabulary and disagree about the substance. They are worth stating as propositions, because most arguments in a metrics review are really a clash between two of them.

The operator school will sign: a cohort curve that flattens above a category benchmark, with each successive cohort flattening higher, is the best available evidence of product-market fit, and the cohort-over-cohort trajectory matters more than the absolute level. It will not sign that flatness proves a permanent floor, though in practice its slides often imply it.

The modelling school — customer-base analysis in the tradition of Peter Fader and Bruce Hardie's shifted-beta-geometric work — will sign something that sounds like sabotage: an aggregate curve flattens as a mathematical consequence of heterogeneity in churn probability, even when no individual user's behaviour changes at all. The apparent floor is a composition effect: the high-hazard users leave first, so the survivors are progressively selected for low hazard, and the observed rate rises toward the lowest hazard present in the population. This school will not sign that flattening indicates habit formation, and will not sign that a floor exists at all.

The demand-side school — Ellis's "how would you feel if you could no longer use this product" survey, and Rahul Vohra's elaboration of it at Superhuman — will sign: product-market fit is a statement about a defined segment's dependence, and retention is a lagging, confounded proxy for it. It will not sign that you can read fit off a chart without knowing who is in the cohort and what they would do instead.

The revenue school, dominant in B2B finance, will sign: in contract businesses the logo curve is nearly uninformative because churn is a discrete renewal event, and net revenue retention with its expansion-contraction decomposition is the signal. It will not sign that user-level curves are the primary instrument for enterprise fit.

The four schools are not reconcilable by synthesis. They disagree about what the curve is evidence of, and a practitioner who cannot say which one they are arguing from will lose the argument to whoever can.

3. Mechanics in depth: the flattening is mostly arithmetic

Begin with the modelling school's claim, because if it is right it changes how the whole chart is read. Suppose Sulagti's March 2025 cohort of 10,000 activated firms contains two invisible segments: 30% who are anchored — the product is inside their filing workflow — with a constant monthly churn probability of 2%; and 70% who are occasional, with a constant monthly churn probability of 40%. No one's behaviour changes over time. Every individual hazard is flat by assumption.

The curve flattens. By month twelve it is losing about half a percentage point a month and any reasonable eye calls it flat. But there is no floor. The occasional segment has simply been exhausted, and what remains is a population decaying at a steady 2% a month forever, with a half-life of ln(0.5)/ln(0.98) = 34 months. The 23.7% reading at month twelve is not a resting place; it is a slide with a shallow gradient. The flattening, in this cohort, carries exactly zero information about habit and complete information about heterogeneity — which is the modelling school's entire point, and it is arithmetically unanswerable.

Two diagnostics separate the cases in practice. The first is to plot the same data on a logarithmic vertical axis. A population with one uniform hazard decays as a pure exponential and appears as a straight line; a heterogeneous population bends upward, its slope flattening as the mix shifts. The second is to stop plotting survival and plot r(t) directly. This is the chart an expert opens first, and most product dashboards do not have it.

Fig. 1. On the linear axis both curves appear to settle, because any decaying quantity approaching a small number looks flat when the y-axis runs to 100. On the log axis the uniform-hazard population is a straight line by construction, while the mixture bends upward as its high-hazard members are exhausted. Visual flatness on a linear plot is therefore not evidence of anything.
Fig. 2. The same cohort, plotted as conditional monthly retention r(t). The rise from 71% to 98% is the composition effect made visible. The two dashed asymptotes are the decision: 98% and 99.7% are visually indistinguishable on a survival chart but differ by a factor of nearly seven in survivor half-life.

The asymptote is the number that matters, and it is estimable long before it is obvious. With 2,369 survivors at month twelve, a hazard of 2.0% produces about 47 departures in the next month and a hazard of 0.3% produces about 7. The standard error on 47 events is roughly √47 ≈ 6.9, so the two hypotheses are distinguishable within a single month of patient observation of the survivors — but only if someone thinks to measure the survivors rather than re-photographing the whole curve.

The financial translation is what earns the analysis its place in a board memo. Expected remaining months for a survivor at constant monthly retention r, over a five-year horizon, is Σt=1..60 rt. At r = 0.98 that sum is 34.4 months; at r = 0.997 it is 54.7. Applied to 2,369 surviving firms at ₹2,400 per month: about ₹19.6 crore of residual revenue against ₹31.1 crore. Same chart, same flatness, a difference of ₹11.5 crore in what the company is worth at that moment. This is why Devika would not sign her chief executive's sentence.

The steps usually left implicit

Four construction choices silently determine the answer, and none of them appear on the chart. The denominator: cohorting by sign-up date blends people who never activated into the base, depressing the floor and hiding whether the loss is pre- or post-activation; cohorting by first core action isolates the question this topic asks. The window: "retained at day 90" can mean active on day 90, active in days 61–90, active at any point in the trailing 90 days, or active at any point ever — and those four definitions can differ by a factor of four on identical data. The re-entry rule: a point-in-time definition lets a returning user re-enter the numerator, which is why some curves tick upward into a "smile"; a continuous definition, once you lapse you are gone, gives a lower and more conservative line. The censoring: only cohorts old enough to have a day-120 observation can contribute to a day-120 comparison, so every long-horizon chart is silently built from the oldest, and often least representative, cohorts.

Only the third and fourth are useful, because only a bounded window in a fixed-length period can decline — the first two are partly cumulative and therefore structurally biased toward flattening. A curve built on a trailing-90-day definition will flatten for a product that is dying, simply because a re-engagement campaign in week ten re-enters a lapsed user into the numerator for the next three months.

4. When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

The retention-curve-as-PMF-signal argument rests on conditions that can be checked before the chart is drawn. Six of them carry most of the weight.

C1. The core need recurs at least twice within the measurement window. If the mean interval between genuine occasions of use is μ, a window shorter than roughly 2μ manufactures churn out of ordinary rhythm. For Sulagti, μ is about 47 days and is clustered around statutory filing dates, so a weekly curve is meaningless and a monthly one is marginal; the defensible cadence is quarterly, calendar-aligned. For Angaarpeth's app, μ is about 30 days, set by the billing cycle, so the monthly window is right. This is the constraint the topic inherits from frequency and intensity of the problem, and it is violated more often than any other.

C2. Cohorts are large enough that tail movement exceeds sampling noise. The standard error on a retained proportion is √(p(1−p)/n). Sulagti's May 2026 cohort has 430 activated firms; at p = 0.24 the standard error is 2.1 percentage points, so a genuine decline of 1.5 points a month is invisible. Angaarpeth's device cohort of 61,000 at p = 0.85 has a standard error of 0.14 points, which is why Prakash can take a two-point move seriously and Devika cannot.

C3. Acquisition mix is stable across the cohorts being compared, or is controlled for. A cohort recruited during a festival discount, an app-store feature, or a channel-partner push is a different population, and comparing its floor to another cohort's measures the channel, not the product.

C4. Leaving is possible and observable. Angaarpeth's device telemetry violates this. A monitor clipped to a meter keeps reporting unless someone physically removes it; the 85% floor measures installation inertia and the absence of a reason to unclip, not continuing value. Where exit requires effort, the curve measures switching cost.

C5. Value accrues per period of use rather than at a single terminal event. For one-shot products — a visa application, a home loan, a wedding registry — the retention curve is not merely uninformative but actively misleading, because success looks identical to abandonment. The right instruments there are completion rate, referral rate and repeat-at-next-occasion, which may be years later.

C6. The user chooses. Where a product is mandated by an employer or a regulator, the curve measures procurement and compliance. A flat line then tells you the contract is in force, which you already knew.

5. Hard edge cases and what mature companies actually do

Two-sided marketplaces. Raakhwaan Mandi, a Nagpur-based platform matching farmer-producer organisations to institutional buyers, tracks supply and demand retention separately, which is standard advice. The non-obvious problem is that the two curves are not independent: a supply cohort's retention is a measure of the demand liquidity that happened to exist while that cohort was young. Raakhwaan's March 2026 FPO cohort joined a thick market and flattened at 41%; the July cohort, joining a thin post-harvest month with the same product, flattened at 12%. The cohort-over-cohort improvement the operator school prizes can therefore be a reading of market conditions, and mature marketplaces control for contemporaneous liquidity on the other side — typically by cohorting on a matched-density band rather than on calendar month — before they claim a product effect.

Fig. 3. Identical product, identical onboarding, identical supply-side segment. The only material difference is the density of active buyers during each cohort's first eight weeks. Marketplace cohort curves are partly a measurement of the other side of the market.

Regulated businesses. Koylaghar Securities, a discount broker, has a dormancy definition imposed from outside: an account with no trade for twelve months is flagged inactive, and reactivation requires re-verification. The retention curve accordingly has a regulator-manufactured cliff at month twelve that is a compliance artefact, not a product event, and a re-KYC step that churns users who fully intended to stay. The mature handling is to keep two curves permanently — a behavioural curve on the product's own core action and a regulatory-status curve — and to never let the second be presented as evidence about the first.

Hardware plus software. Angaarpeth's split is the canonical case and Fig. 4 below makes it concrete. A device curve and an app curve on the same cohort describe different products with different economics: the device floor sets warranty and replacement planning, the app floor sets everything subscription-shaped.

AI-native products. Three complications compound. Novelty decay is unusually steep, because the first week of an assistant is a demo and weeks four to eight are the test. The model changes underneath the cohorts, so a cohort comparison confounds product improvement with a vendor's model upgrade — Sulagti's January and April cohorts differ by two model versions and one prompt rewrite, and no amount of cohort discipline separates them retrospectively. And marginal cost is not zero: a flat curve at a low floor can be an actively loss-making floor once inference cost per retained user is charged against it. Sulagti's retained firms cost ₹310 a month in inference against ₹2,400 in revenue, which is fine; a consumer AI product flattening at 8% with ₹40 of monthly inference per retained user often is not.

Multi-product and the organisational seams. Dhuaanrekha Health runs a medication log and a teleconsult module. Users of both retain at 47% against 14% for the log alone, and the obvious reading — push module two — is wrong in an instructive way. Of the 1,900 dual-module users, 78% adopted the second module after day 45, meaning they were already survivors when they adopted. Restricting to users who adopted module two within seven days and matching on activation depth, the floor is 19% against a matched 14% — real, worth having, and a quarter of the headline. The seam matters institutionally too: at Dhuaanrekha the growth team owned days 1–7, the product team owned day 30, and customer success owned renewals, and each maintained its own definition of "active". Mature companies solve this not with better analysts but with a metric-definition registry: one owner per definition, version-stamped, with a rule that any change forces a full historical recomputation before the new curve is shown next to the old.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

They open the hazard chart before the survival chart. The competent practitioner looks at S(t) and asks whether it has flattened; the expert looks at r(t) and asks what it is converging to. The tell in a meeting is the question "what is the monthly retention among the people who are still here?" — a question the survival chart cannot answer and the hazard chart answers immediately. The obvious reading is wrong because flatness in S(t) is nearly guaranteed once S(t) is small, whatever the underlying hazard.

They treat flatness as a claim about composition, not commitment. When a curve flattens, the expert's first hypothesis is that the cohort's high-hazard members have been exhausted, not that the survivors have formed a habit. The tell is that they immediately ask for the curve split by an a-priori segment, because if the flattening is a mixture effect the segments will have visibly different curves and the blended one will lie between them.

They know the floor's altitude is a separate question from its existence. A curve flat at 3% and a curve flat at 60% pass the identical statistical test. Whether the floor supports a business depends on contribution margin, acquisition cost and addressable market — facts the curve does not contain. The tell is that they never say "we have PMF" without saying what the floor is worth.

They demand cohort size with every floor. A floor quoted without an n is not a finding. Experts carry the standard-error arithmetic in their head well enough to know that a 400-person cohort cannot distinguish flat from a slow slide, and they will refuse to compare a recent small cohort to an old large one as though the comparison were symmetrical.

They ask what the window does to the shape before asking what the shape means. Given an unfamiliar curve, the expert's first three questions are the denominator, the window and the re-entry rule. The tell is discomfort at any curve that rises: a genuine survival curve under a continuous definition cannot rise, so an upward tick means either re-entry is allowed or the cohort definition is leaking.

They read the cadence off the problem, not off the dashboard. The natural frequency of the underlying need sets the measurement period; the dashboard's default of daily, weekly and monthly sets nothing. An expert measuring a quarterly-frequency product on a monthly cadence knows they are looking at a chart of the calendar, and says so before anyone else notices.

They separate the curve's level from its trajectory across cohorts. One flat curve is a fact about one cohort; a sequence of cohorts flattening at progressively higher floors is evidence the team is learning. The obvious reading — that the newest cohort's floor is the current truth — is wrong because the newest cohort is the youngest and therefore the least censored-corrected and the most exposed to whatever acquisition experiment was running.

They distinguish inertia from value. Where leaving is costly, difficult or invisible — installed hardware, embedded enterprise software, an account with a balance in it — the curve measures friction. The tell is that experts pair every such curve with an intensity measure: not just whether the user is present, but how much of the core action they perform per period, because falling intensity behind a flat curve is the leading indicator of a cliff.

They are specific about what would change their mind. Before running the analysis, an expert states the floor and the survivor hazard that would make them abandon the segment. The tell is that the threshold exists in writing beforehand; otherwise the curve will be interpreted to support whatever was already decided, and it usually is.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the individual decides alone and the need usually recurs weekly or faster, so a curve can be read at eight to twelve weeks and the daily or weekly cadence is genuinely informative. In B2B and enterprise the curve's shape changes character: churn is a discrete renewal event, so the honest instrument is a stepped curve at renewal boundaries plus net revenue retention within surviving accounts, and a seat-level daily curve mostly measures which individuals inside the account happen to be the workflow's operators. Sulagti sits awkwardly between the two — sold to small firms on monthly terms, used by named individuals — which is exactly why both Devika's cohort curve and a renewal-boundary view are needed.

For platforms and marketplaces the difference is real and structural: two coupled populations, cohorts that are not independent of each other, and liquidity as a confounder, as Raakhwaan demonstrates. For hardware the difference is also real: two curves, one of which measures installation and one of which measures engagement, plus a replacement cycle that puts a ceiling on any floor. For AI products, contrary to a good deal of current commentary, the underlying statistics are not special; what is special is the steeper novelty decay, the non-trivial marginal cost per retained user, and the moving model beneath the cohorts. It is worth saying plainly that the mathematics of survival does not change for AI, and claims that it requires a new framework are usually claims that the author's curve looks bad.

Stage changes the use, not the method. A pre-Series-A company uses the curve existentially — is there anything here at all — and can tolerate small cohorts and crude definitions because the signal it is hunting is large. A scaled company already knows it has fit in aggregate and uses the identical technique at fine grain: one segment, one market, one redesign, where the effects are small, the cohorts are large, and definitional discipline is the whole game.

8. Three worked examples

Angaarpeth Energy: two curves, one cohort

Fig. 4. Angaarpeth Energy, installation cohort of 61,000 units. Both curves flatten; they describe different products. The device curve satisfies no version of condition C4 — the user cannot easily leave — while the app curve does.

Prakash's growth lead had modelled the ₹99 Plus tier against the device floor: 85% of 61,000 is 51,850 households, a conversion assumption of 12% gives 6,222 subscribers and ₹6.2 lakh a month. Against the app floor the same assumption gives 4,270 engaged users and, at 12%, 512 subscribers — ₹51,000 a month against a build cost Prakash estimated at ₹1.4 crore. But segmenting the app curve rescued the strategy: households flattened at 4.1%, while the 5,500 small textile units in Tiruppur flattened at 34%, because for a power-loom operator the app answers a question with money attached to it — which shift is burning the most units. A ₹499 business tier sold into 1,870 engaged units at 30% conversion is ₹2.8 lakh a month from a far smaller build. The segmentation, not the curve, produced the decision.

Sulagti Labs: estimating the asymptote instead of eyeballing the floor

Devika's team had the March 2025 cohort at 23.7% and stable. Rather than argue about the word "flat", she measured the survivors. Over months twelve to fifteen the cohort fell from 2,369 to 2,201 — a compound conditional retention of (2201/2369)1/3 = 97.6% a month, with roughly 168 departures observed against a standard error near 13, comfortably distinguishable from the 0.3% hazard that would have justified the chief executive's sentence. At 97.6% the survivors' half-life is 28 months, and the five-year residual is ₹19.6 crore rather than ₹31.1 crore. The finding was not that Sulagti lacked fit; it was that the anchored segment was real but leaking, and that a 1.3-point reduction in monthly hazard was worth more than any new cohort the growth budget could buy.

Dhuaanrekha Health: the failure, and the recovery

In late 2024 Dhuaanrekha presented a curve flattening at 34% and used it to justify tripling its field sales team for a chronic-care contract push, spending roughly ₹11 crore over three quarters. The curve was built on the "any session in the trailing 90 days" definition from Table 2, and the company was running monthly re-engagement pushes; every push re-entered lapsed users into a three-month-wide numerator, and the curve flattened because the definition would not let it fall. When a new analytics lead rebuilt it on a bounded 30-day window with the core action as a logged dose, the same cohorts flattened at 11% and were still declining at month nine. The contracts signed on the strength of the 34% number renewed at 38%.

The recovery took fourteen months and had three parts. First, every historical cohort was recomputed on the bounded definition and the old charts were destroyed rather than deprecated, because two definitions circulating in one company guarantees the flattering one survives. Second, the curve was cut by condition, and the diabetes cohort was found to flatten at 38% on the strict definition while the general-wellness cohort flattened at 4%; the company narrowed to diabetes and cut two modules. Third, re-engagement campaigns were excluded from the retention definition entirely and reported as a separate resurrection curve, so that marketing activity could no longer masquerade as product value. The instructive part is that no one at Dhuaanrekha lied. The definition did the lying, and no one owned it.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and the cost of catching them late

Table 3. Recurring failure modes in retention-curve practice.

The pattern across the table is that each failure is cheap to catch at the moment the chart is built and expensive to catch after a decision has been made on it, because by then the number is in a memo, an operating plan or a term sheet, and correcting it is a political act rather than an analytical one. The single most useful institutional habit is a written definition attached to every published curve, with an owner's name on it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does a floor exist at all? The operator school holds that products with real fit develop a durable core whose hazard approaches zero, and points to decade-old consumer products with cohorts still active. The modelling school holds that this is the visible tail of a heterogeneous population and that no zero-hazard segment has ever been demonstrated; every apparently permanent cohort, followed long enough, keeps losing 1–3% a year. For the modelling school to be wrong, one would need a cohort observed over many years whose conditional retention reached and stayed at 100% within sampling error — which, notably, nobody has published. For the operator school to be wrong in a way that matters, the residual hazard would have to be large enough to change investment decisions, which at 2% a month it is and at 0.2% a year it is not. The honest position is that the disagreement is about magnitude and that both sides should be quoting the asymptote.

Is the curve the primary PMF instrument, or a lagging proxy? The demand-side school argues that retention is downstream of a fact about a segment, is confounded by switching cost and acquisition mix, and arrives too late to steer an early product; its evidence is cases where a survey identified a high-affinity segment months before the curve did. The curve school replies that surveys measure stated preference from people still present, which is survivorship by another name, and that the curve measures behaviour. For the demand-side school to be wrong, segment surveys would have to fail to predict subsequent cohort floors; for the curve school to be wrong, curves would have to be systematically unreadable at the stage when decisions are made — which C2's arithmetic suggests is sometimes literally true for small cohorts.

Logos or revenue? The revenue school holds that in contract businesses a logo curve can flatten while the business shrinks, or fall while the business grows, and that net revenue retention is therefore the only honest instrument. The counter-argument is that revenue retention can be held up by price increases and expansion into a shrinking base of accounts, hiding a fit problem for two or three renewal cycles. Both are documented. The practical resolution most large firms reach is to publish both and to treat any divergence between them as the finding.

How long must you wait? Common practice says three times the natural frequency period; some practitioners insist on nothing less than a full year for anything sold annually. The disagreement is not really empirical — it is about the cost of waiting. A company with eighteen months of runway that waits twelve months for a defensible curve has made a decision by not deciding.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces a correct chart and a confident sentence. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four visible ways. They instrument the core action before the feature ships, not after the question is asked, because a cohort cannot be reconstructed retrospectively from events nobody logged. They hold two curves at once as a matter of routine — logos and revenue, device and app, behavioural and regulatory — and treat the gap between them as the interesting quantity. They quote floors with their cohort size and their definition in the same breath, which sounds pedantic and is the fastest way to end an unproductive argument. And they know the short list of decisions the curve cannot inform: how large the market is, what the users will pay, whether a competitor is about to make the floor irrelevant. The mark of the expert is not producing a better curve; it is the speed with which they say "this chart cannot answer that question" and name the one that can.

12. The decisions

Devika wrote a different sentence: "Sulagti's March 2025 cohort has an anchored segment of roughly 2,350 firms retaining at 97.6% a month, implying a five-year residual of about ₹19.6 crore; the curve has flattened, but the segment is leaking at 28-month half-life and the extension should be sized on that." She added a hazard chart to the monthly review, put a written threshold in place — if survivor hazard does not fall below 1.5% a month within two quarters, the enterprise expansion is deferred — and redirected two engineers from acquisition-funnel work onto the renewal hazard. The reasoning was that at Sulagti's stage the largest available gain was not another cohort but a lower asymptote on the cohorts already bought and paid for.

Prakash killed the ₹99 consumer tier and approved the ₹499 business tier for textile units, with a board deck that from then on carried the device and app curves side by side under separate headings and never a blended "retention" figure. He also commissioned an intensity measure behind the device curve — reports viewed per active unit per month — on the grounds that an 85% floor which he could not explain was a liability rather than an asset. Both decisions rest on the same move: refusing to let one flat line stand for the whole product.

Discussion questions

1. Devika's cohort satisfies every textbook test for a flattened curve, yet she declined to claim product-market fit. Was she right, or has she set a standard that no early-stage company could ever meet in time to act on it?

2. Angaarpeth's device curve flattens at 85% because users cannot easily leave. Under what circumstances, if any, is a retention curve driven by switching cost still legitimate evidence of fit?

3. If the modelling school is right that flattening is pure composition, what would you replace "does the curve flatten?" with as the one question a board should ask a product team about fit?

13. Going deeper

Cohort analysis — the construction underneath the curve; controls how cohorts are cut, censored and compared.

Frequency and intensity of the problem — sets the cadence and the expected shape; the constraint violated most often.

Stickiness and natural frequency — separates today's usage habit from whether a cohort is still present at all.

Churn analysis — moves from the shape of the curve to the named reasons individual users leave.

Modelling LTV from retention — turns the asymptote into the rupee figure that decides investment.

Product-market fit — the broader construct the curve is evidence for, including the demand-side instruments.

Retention strategy — the interventions that raise a floor or lower a survivor hazard, and how to sequence them.

Decomposing retention changes — separates product effect from acquisition-mix effect when a floor moves.

Constructing a funnel — the pre-cohort view; determines who ever reaches the curve's starting line.

Reading drop-off — locates where the steep early decline happens and whether it is fixable.

Defining activation (the aha moment) — fixes the core action and therefore the cohort's denominator.

Feature adoption analysis — tests whether a shipped change reaches the users whose hazard you meant to lower.

Segmenting users in analytics — the move that rescued Angaarpeth; turns a blended floor into actionable ones.

Root cause analysis of a metric change — the discipline for when a floor moves and nobody knows why.

Retention Curves and the PMF Signal

On the morning of Monday, 9 February 2026, Ritika Bhalla, Director of Product at Dridhkosh Money, opened the slide she would present to the board on Thursday and deleted it. Dridhkosh sold a simple idea to gig-economy delivery riders and kirana shop owners across Bengaluru, Indore and Surat: a recurring micro-deposit, debited automatically after every UPI payment they received, that rounded up to the nearest ten rupees and swept the difference into a locked savings pot. The company had 340,000 app downloads, 96,000 users who had opened an account, and roughly 41,000 monthly active users. Those numbers, printed large, looked like momentum. But Dridhkosh was raising a Series B, and the lead investor's associate had asked a plainer question over email the previous week: "Do you have product-market fit, or do you have referral bonuses?" Ritika's old slide answered with downloads and MAU. She knew, uneasily, that neither number could answer the question being asked.

What the associate wanted to know was whether the people who tried Dridhkosh kept using it once the novelty and the sign-up bonus wore off. Growth fuelled by advertising and referral credits can make almost any download count rise for a while; only the behaviour of people already inside the product, tracked over time, reveals whether they are staying because the product solves something real. Ritika had the raw data to answer this. What she needed was the right way to look at it, and the discipline to say what it did and did not prove before she stood in front of people who would fund, or not fund, the next two years of Dridhkosh's life.

The idea

A retention curve plots the percentage of a cohort of users — people who started using a product at roughly the same time — who are still performing its core value action as time passes since they started. Each cohort produces one line: it begins at 100% on day zero and falls as some users stop, day by day or week by week. The question a retention curve exists to answer is not "how many users do we have" but "of the users we already earned, how many decided to stay" — and, crucially, whether that falling line eventually stops falling. A curve that keeps declining toward zero, however slowly, says the product has not yet found a natural floor: given enough time, everyone leaves. A curve that bends and settles onto a horizontal line says something different: a stable core of users has decided this is now a habit or a dependency, and that floor, not the peak, is the honest size of what has been built.

The technique descends from survival analysis in actuarial science and epidemiology, where researchers have long plotted the fraction of a population still alive, still employed, or still disease-free over time. Digital product teams adapted the same logic in the early-to-mid 2010s, when consumer growth teams at companies including Facebook and later a wave of Silicon Valley startups needed a way to separate real engagement from acquisition noise. The framing was sharpened and popularised through the startup operating literature of that period — writers and growth practitioners such as Brian Balfour and Andrew Chen, building on Sean Ellis's earlier product-market-fit survey work — into the specific claim this topic is built around: a flattening cohort retention curve is the closest thing product management has to hard evidence of product-market fit. The sentence Ritika could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: "If the line keeps falling forever, we've built a leaky bucket with good marketing; if it bends and holds, the water that's left has decided to stay."

How it actually works

Building a retention curve correctly involves several steps, and the ones practitioners skip are usually the ones that make the difference between a useful chart and a misleading one. First, define the core action precisely — not "opened the app" but the behaviour that actually carries the product's value. For Dridhkosh, that was a completed recurring-deposit instalment, not a login. Second, form cohorts by the date users first performed that core action, not the date they signed up; signing up and never depositing is a different failure than depositing once and stopping, and blending the two understates a curve that is really about activated users. Third, for each cohort, calculate the percentage of the original cohort size still performing the core action within each subsequent period — day 7, day 30, day 60, and so on — using a consistent definition of "active in this window" across every cohort being compared. Fourth, plot each cohort as its own line against days or weeks elapsed, rather than collapsing everyone into one blended number.

The step most newcomers leave implicit is the fifth one: overlay several cohorts side by side, ideally from different months, and ask two separate questions of the picture at once. Does each individual line eventually go flat? And do later cohorts flatten at a higher floor than earlier ones? The first question tells you whether the product has found any floor at all. The second tells you whether the product is getting better at creating one — whether changes the team is shipping are actually moving the number that matters, rather than just moving downloads. A single flat line, on its own, is a weaker claim than most people treat it as; a rising floor across successive cohorts is the real signal of a team learning its way toward product-market fit rather than having stumbled onto it once.

A worked example

Ritika pulled two cohorts. The first was users who completed their first recurring deposit in the week of 6 October 2025, before Dridhkosh shipped an autopay-reminder feature in December that nudged users by SMS when their UPI mandate was about to lapse. The second was users who completed their first deposit in the week of 5 January 2026, after that feature had shipped to everyone.

The arithmetic behind the flattening claim is what makes it defensible rather than asserted: 610 divided by 5,000 is 12.2%, and 615 divided by 5,000 is 12.3% — a movement of one tenth of a percentage point between day 90 and day 120, which is noise, not decline. The same test on the January cohort, 1,364 divided by 5,200 against 1,370 divided by 5,200, gives 26.2% against 26.3% — equally flat. Both curves have found a floor. Now change one input: suppose Ritika had looked only at day 30, as an impatient version of this analysis might. Day 30 shows 23.0% against 40.0%, a real improvement, but day 30 alone cannot distinguish a floor from a curve still sliding toward zero more slowly than before — the October cohort was still losing more than 45% of its remaining users between day 30 and day 90. Only the near-zero slope from day 90 to day 120, on both lines, licenses the word "flat." The feature did not just move one number; it moved the floor the whole curve rests on, and that is the fact worth taking to a board.

The nuances

Flattening is about slope, not altitude

A curve that goes flat at 3% has technically flattened, and a curve that goes flat at 60% has too; the statistical test is the same, but the business conclusion is not. "Flat" tells you a floor exists; it says nothing about whether that floor is high enough to build a company on. Whether 26% is enough for Dridhkosh is a judgment about unit economics and market size, not a fact the curve itself supplies.

Slowing down is not the same as stopping

A curve that falls more slowly than it used to can look, over a short window, like it is flattening. Distinguishing genuine flattening from merely decelerated decay requires enough elapsed time — commonly two to three times the length of the product's natural usage cycle — before the claim is safe to make at all.

Cohort by first value, not by signup

Cohorting by the date someone registered, rather than the date they first performed the core action, mixes people who never really started using the product into the denominator. This makes an otherwise healthy curve look worse than it is and obscures where the real drop-off happens: before or after activation.

The problem's natural frequency sets the expected shape

A curve should be read against how often the underlying need actually recurs. A tax-filing product will show a curve that looks like near-total churn on a weekly cadence yet retain the same households faithfully every year; measuring on the wrong cadence turns real, infrequent loyalty into an apparent collapse.

Aggregate growth can hide cohort decay

A rising company-wide monthly-active-user count can coexist with every individual cohort decaying badly, if new user acquisition is large enough to backfill the losses. Only cohort-by-cohort curves, overlaid, expose this; the blended topline number is compatible with either a healthy or a dying product.

It cannot tell you about the market or the money

A beautifully flat curve says a slice of people who tried the product stayed. It says nothing about whether that slice is large enough, willing to pay enough, or cheap enough to acquire, to be a viable business. Product-market fit in the retention-curve sense is necessary evidence, not sufficient proof.

It is not the same thing as a stickiness ratio

DAU/MAU and similar stickiness ratios describe how often an existing user base returns within a given period; a retention curve describes whether a specific cohort, tracked since it joined, keeps shrinking or has stopped. They are related, frequently confused, and answer different questions — one about today's habit, the other about whether people who arrived together are still there.

Consumer, B2B and marketplace, early stage and scale

In a consumer product like Dridhkosh, the individual decides alone, usage is frequent, and a curve can meaningfully flatten or fail to within eight to twelve weeks, which is why Ritika could already form a view on cohorts three to four months old. A B2B product sold on annual contracts behaves differently: churn happens in discrete events at renewal, not as a smooth daily leak, so a stepped curve measured at renewal boundaries, alongside net revenue retention within surviving accounts, matters more than a daily-active line. Thambgrid, a workforce-scheduling platform sold to warehouse operators, would see almost no curve movement for eleven months and then a cliff at contract renewal — a shape the consumer framing would misread as either perfect retention or sudden catastrophic failure, when it is neither.

A marketplace complicates the picture further because it has two populations whose fates are entangled. Langarhaat, a marketplace pairing truck owners with shippers, has to track supply-side and demand-side retention as separate curves, because a truck owner who leaves for lack of loads and a shipper who leaves for lack of available trucks are different failures needing different fixes, and each side's curve shape depends on how liquid the other side is. Stage matters too: an early company like Dridhkosh uses the retention curve to answer the existential question of whether it has built anything worth funding at all, while a large, established company no longer in doubt about that uses the identical technique at a much narrower grain — testing one redesign, one new market, or one segment at a time.

Common mistakes

Declaring victory from a seven-day curve

The symptom is a confident retention slide built entirely from week-one data. The underlying error is mistaking onboarding enthusiasm for durable value, since almost any reasonably designed product holds people for their first week. The cheapest check is to replot the identical cohort at day 60 or 90 before repeating the claim in front of anyone who can act on it.

Reading one blended, all-time number

A single company-wide "30-day retention: 34%" figure that barely moves month to month looks reassuring precisely because it hides the underlying trend. It blends cohorts of different ages, channels and vintages into one average. The fix is to break it into cohort-by-signup-period curves, overlaid, so improvement or decay in either direction becomes visible.

Counting the wrong action as retained

A curve can look healthy while revenue or task completion quietly does not follow it, when "retained" was defined as any app open rather than the action that actually produces value. The diagnostic is to redefine the retained event around the core action and see whether the curve still flattens at the same floor.

Comparing across a promotional spike

A cohort acquired during a referral-bonus or festival campaign often shows a lower floor and gets read, wrongly, as evidence the product itself regressed. The real cause is usually a shift in acquisition-channel mix, which changes who is in the cohort, not how good the product is. Segmenting the spiked cohort by channel before comparing it to others catches this cheaply.

What good looks like

Eighteen months earlier, Meher Kohli, product lead at Aadharshila Learning, a foundational-literacy app for children in tier-two and tier-three towns, faced the identical question from her own board. Rather than presenting one blended retention figure, she insisted on waiting until every cohort under discussion was at least 120 days old, split each cohort by acquisition source — school partnerships versus paid app-install advertising — and presented three separate lines instead of one average. The school-partnership cohort flattened at 44% weekly-active by day 120; the paid-install cohort flattened at 9%. That evidence, not a single downloads number, let Aadharshila's board redirect its next funding round toward expanding school partnerships nationally rather than spending more on paid acquisition. The discipline was not exotic: patience for the curve to age, cohorts split by the variable that mattered, and a willingness to show the board an uncomfortable low number alongside the encouraging one.

Closing

Ritika rebuilt her slide around exactly this pair of curves: the 12% floor before the autopay-reminder feature, the 26% floor after it, both confirmed flat by day 120, with a third, newer cohort from February already tracking the same rising path. She told the board plainly that 12% alone would not have justified a Series B, and that downloads and MAU had never been the real evidence either way. She recommended the new capital go toward deepening the autopay mechanic across the existing base rather than toward more paid acquisition, and she flagged, honestly, that two more cohorts were needed to confirm the 26% floor was structural rather than a temporary novelty effect. Her next steps sat exactly where this topic points: churn analysis, to understand who still leaves within that 26%, and decomposing retention changes, to separate how much of the lift came from the feature itself versus a shift in who Dridhkosh was acquiring during that window.

Two questions worth sitting with:

1. How many periods of cohort data would you personally need to see before you would call a curve "flat" in front of your own board — and what would make you wait longer?

2. If two products both show a flattening retention curve, what is the one further number you would ask for before deciding which represents the healthier business?

Praman: The Night Before the Board

Case lens: retention curves and the product-market-fit signal. The case does not name the answer, and the exhibits do not agree with one another.

1. Sunday night, Powai

At 11.20 on the night of Sunday, 13 September 2026, Shalini Deshmukh was in the third-floor conference room of Praman's office in Powai, Mumbai, with the monsoon still coming off the lake and the air conditioning off because the building's night settings could not be overridden. Spread across the table were four printouts, none of which she was willing to put in front of the board at nine the next morning.

The first showed that Praman's self-serve retention curve had flattened at 41 per cent and had held there for seven months. The second showed the same cohorts with a single line of instrumentation removed, and the floor at 17 per cent and still descending. The third showed enterprise logo retention at 97 per cent and net revenue retention at 126 per cent. The fourth showed that the number of documents processed per active enterprise account had fallen 38 per cent in eleven months.

Praman had ₹22 crore in the bank, ninety-six employees across four countries, and a bridge term sheet for ₹85 crore that expired on 30 September. The lead investor's diligence request, received on Friday evening, contained one line that Shalini had read perhaps thirty times: please share monthly cohort retention for all revenue lines, on a consistent activity definition, for the last eighteen months. She had two such definitions, three data sources, and one very large customer whose usage she could not observe at all.

2. Praman, and the decision that still binds it

Praman was founded in 2021 by Shalini and Nikhil Vartak, who had worked together on a lending stack before that. The product read documents: KYC packets, bank statements, GST returns, salary slips, invoices, property papers. It extracted fields, checked them against each other and against public registries, flagged the inconsistencies, and produced an auditable verification record. Indian lenders, non-banking financial companies and insurers were the buyers. The first version was rules and optical character recognition; the 2024 rebuild put a language model at the centre and renamed the flagship module Praman Copilot.

The decision that constrains everything today was taken in March 2023. Aravali Finserv, a Mumbai-headquartered NBFC with ₹31,000 crore of assets under management, was prepared to sign a ₹9.8 crore annual contract on one condition: Praman would deploy inside Aravali's own virtual private cloud, with no outbound telemetry of any kind. Aravali's compliance team, reading the Reserve Bank of India's outsourcing and digital-lending guidance conservatively, would not accept a vendor emitting usage events from a system touching borrower documents. Nikhil signed. It was, at the time, the difference between a company and a project.

Three years later, seven of Praman's eleven enterprise accounts, and 62 per cent of its revenue, sat behind that same clause. Praman knew what those customers paid. It did not know what they did. Usage reporting from the dark deployments arrived as a quarterly CSV, prepared by each customer's own IT team, with no agreed definition of what counted as a processed document and no way to audit it.

3. The industry around it

The market Praman sold into had been reshaped three times in five years. The account aggregator framework had made consented financial data available through a regulated pipe, reducing the need to read a bank statement as a PDF at all. DigiLocker and the Central KYC Registry had done something similar for identity documents. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 had made every lender cautious about where borrower documents were processed, which helped Praman's on-premise story and hurt its cloud one. The GST network had made business financials machine-readable for anyone with a taxpayer's consent.

The competitive set was serious and well capitalised. Perfios, Signzy and IDfy had all built substantial positions in Indian financial-document infrastructure, and the market treated them as the reference points. Setu and Yubi had made parts of the stack available as APIs. Below all of them sat an uncomfortable fact: the cost of reading a page with a general-purpose model had fallen by roughly 85 per cent in twenty months, which meant that a competent engineering team at any large lender could now build eighty per cent of Praman's extraction capability in a quarter. Whether the remaining twenty per cent — the reconciliation logic, the audit record, the two thousand edge cases of Indian document formats — was a business or a feature was the question nobody at Praman said out loud.

Praman's global exposure ran through two doors. Rashid Finance House in Dubai had signed in 2025 for ₹4.4 crore a year, attracted by Praman's handling of Arabic and English mixed-script salary certificates, and had since become the reference account for the Gulf. And Derek Almeida, hired in New Jersey in late 2025, had been selling a cloud version to American mid-market lenders on the argument that Indian document complexity made the product over-engineered for the United States and therefore very reliable there.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The self-serve tier launched in January 2024 at ₹2,999 per month for 500 documents, aimed at small NBFCs, direct-selling agents and fintech startups that could not afford an enterprise contract. It grew steadily and unspectacularly to 1,840 paying accounts by December 2025, contributing ₹6.6 crore of annual recurring revenue.

In February 2026, Dr Anirban Sen, who led data science from Toronto, presented a cohort chart at the quarterly review showing that self-serve monthly retention had fallen to 41 per cent by month four and then held there through month twelve. It was the first flat curve anyone at Praman had produced. Nikhil put it in the January investor update under the heading Product-market fit, demonstrated. The company hired four more self-serve growth people and raised the paid-acquisition budget from ₹40 lakh to ₹1.9 crore a quarter.

Two things have since turned out to be wrong. The first was found in June 2026 by Kavya Ramaswamy, a data engineer in Bengaluru, while investigating an unrelated billing discrepancy. Praman's activity definition counted any authenticated API call as activity. A large share of self-serve accounts were integrated through a handful of Indian fintech platform vendors whose connectors issued a scheduled health-check call every six hours, authenticated with the customer's key, whether or not any document was processed. Once health-check calls were excluded and activity was redefined as at least one document successfully verified, the floor moved from 41 per cent to 17 per cent, and the last four months of the curve resumed descending.

The second was subtler and is still contested. The February chart had been produced by averaging the columns of the cohort triangle rather than reading its rows. Because the newest cohorts were the largest and had only three or four observed months, the later columns were disproportionately made of older, better cohorts. Anirban maintains that the effect is worth three to five points, not twenty-four, and that the health-check bug is the whole story. Kavya's reconstruction puts the column effect at nine points. They have not reconciled, and both reconstructions appear in the board pack.

Meanwhile, on the enterprise side, two of the eleven accounts — a Chennai insurer and a Pune-based housing finance company, together ₹7.1 crore — have indicated that they will “re-scope” at renewal. Both have excellent logo-retention histories and both have paid on time for three years. When Meera Pillai, the customer-success lead in Singapore, asked why, the Pune answer was that their own engineering team had built statement parsing in-house over the last two quarters and would keep Praman only for the audit record.

8. The options as Shalini currently sees them

Option A — enterprise only. Shut the self-serve tier, redeploy fourteen engineers to on-premise delivery, present logo retention and net revenue retention as the fit evidence, and raise the bridge on a story of eleven large accounts and a defensible compliance position. It is clean, it is what Nikhil wants, and it removes the need to restate anything, since the self-serve line would no longer exist. It also means the company's only evidence of fit is a set of renewals it cannot observe, in a segment where one customer has already built the core capability in-house.

Option B — fix the measurement first. Tell the board that Praman does not currently know its retention, commit to a rebuilt event store and a single published definition within ninety days, and ask for the bridge on the strength of candour and enterprise revenue. Rajat has said privately that he respects this kind of disclosure. He has not said what his investment committee will do with it in the same quarter the fund marked the company up.

Option C — re-price and re-aim self-serve. Keep the tier but move it to usage-based pricing at ₹4 per verified document, on the theory that the 17 per cent floor is an artefact of a subscription that people forget to cancel and that a usage-priced cohort would reveal true demand within two months. This is the only option that generates new information quickly. It also cuts self-serve revenue immediately and needs engineers Farah does not have.

Shalini has written all three on a whiteboard twice and erased them twice. Her difficulty is that all three assume the unit of analysis is the account. Praman's product is not used by accounts; it is used inside a loan file, by an operations analyst, for a particular document type, at a particular step. It is possible that the right curve is drawn per workflow — the share of a lender's loan files that still route through Praman in month N — and that both 41 and 17 are answers to a question nobody needed. She has no instrumentation for that curve, and building it inside a dark deployment would require reopening the March 2023 clause with Aravali's compliance team.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The bridge term sheet expires on 30 September. It carries a condition that no previously reported metric be materially restated before close, which Nikhil has read and Shalini has now read. Praman has ₹22 crore of cash and a monthly burn of ₹2.4 crore, giving roughly nine months without the bridge and eighteen with it. Aravali's contract requires ninety days' notice of renewal terms, which falls due on 1 October, and contains a delivery milestone that Farah says slips if self-serve keeps its fourteen engineers. The telemetry clause cannot be varied without Aravali's compliance sign-off, a process their own team estimates at four months. Ninety-six people are employed across Mumbai, Bengaluru, Pune, Toronto, Singapore, Berlin and New Jersey; the Berlin and New Jersey salary bands mean that a ten per cent headcount reduction taken there saves what a thirty per cent reduction saves in Pune, a fact Farah has mentioned once and nobody has picked up. The board meets at nine on Monday 14 September.
